label: Diffuse_Large_B_Cell_Lymphoma_NOS
query: Diffuse Large B Cell Lymphoma NOS
answer_markdown:
## Key Facts

- Most common adult non-Hodgkin lymphoma (~30%); median age in seventh decade, but occurs across all ages
- Defined by diffuse proliferation of medium to large atypical B cells not meeting criteria for other large B-cell lymphomas ([WHO](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/WHO/WHO_HTML/PEDS/Diffuse_Large_B_Cell_Lymphoma_Nos.html), [Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/lymphomadiffuse.html))
- Subtyped as germinal center B cell (GCB) or activated B cell (ABC) by IHC/Hans algorithm; this impacts prognosis
- Exclude high-grade B cell lymphoma with MYC and BCL2 and/or BCL6 rearrangements (double/triple hit) before diagnosis
- High Ki-67, pan B-cell markers (CD20, CD19, PAX5, CD79a); negative for TdT, ALK, cyclin D1 ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/lymphomadiffuse.html))

## Terminology

- Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, NOS (DLBCL-NOS): Neoplasm of mature blastic B-cells with diffuse growth, lacking features of other large B-cell lymphoma subtypes ([WHO](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/WHO/WHO_HTML/PEDS/Diffuse_Large_B_Cell_Lymphoma_Nos.html), [Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/lymphomadiffuse.html))
- Synonyms: None; abbreviation "DLBCL-NOS" is standard
- Not recommended/obsolete: "large B-cell lymphoma, diffuse" or "centroblastic/immunoblastic lymphoma"

## Essential and Desirable Diagnostic Criteria

- **Essential:**
  - Diffuse effacement by a proliferation of medium to large lymphoid cells with centroblastic and/or immunoblastic morphology ([WHO](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/WHO/WHO_HTML/PEDS/Diffuse_Large_B_Cell_Lymphoma_Nos.html), [Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/lymphomadiffuse.html))
  - Mature B-cell immunophenotype: CD20+, CD19+, PAX5+, CD79a+; negative for TdT, ALK, cyclin D1, and CD3 ([WHO](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/WHO/WHO_HTML/PEDS/Diffuse_Large_B_Cell_Lymphoma_Nos.html), [Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/lymphomadiffuse.html))
  - High proliferation index (Ki-67), typically high
  - Cell nuclei ≥ the size of histiocyte or 2× normal lymphocyte nuclei
  - Does not meet criteria for other WHO-defined large B-cell lymphoma categories (require workup to exclude high-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC and BCL2/BCL6 rearrangements; ALK+ DLBCL; PMBCL; etc.)
  - GCB vs ABC workup (IHC/Hans algorithm or gene expression profiling) required
- **Desirable:**
  - Ki-67 index <95% ([WHO](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/WHO/WHO_HTML/PEDS/Diffuse_Large_B_Cell_Lymphoma_Nos.html))
  - Absence of MYC, BCL2, or BCL6 rearrangements by FISH; if present, diagnose as HGBL ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/lymphomadiffuse.html))
  - Genetic testing for relevant mutations
  - EBER ISH; if >80% cells positive, classify as EBV+ DLBCL, NOS ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/lymphomadiffuse.html))

## Etiology/Pathogenesis

- May arise de novo or by transformation from low-grade B-cell lymphomas (e.g., follicular lymphoma, CLL/SLL, marginal zone lymphoma, nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma) ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/lymphomadiffuse.html))
- Molecular subtypes:
  - Activated B cell (ABC): MYD88 L265P, CD79B, NOTCH2 mutations; ~40% of cases
  - Germinal center B cell (GCB): BCL2 rearrangements (~20–30%), EZH2 mutations, other chromatin modifiers (~60%)
  - BCL6 rearrangement in ~30% (more common in ABC)
  - MYC rearrangement in 8–14% (about half also have BCL2/BCL6 co-rearrangement/double hit)
  - TP53 mutation ~9%
  - Heterogeneous mutational landscape (>150 genes implicated)
- Can be associated with chronic inflammation, e.g., pleural DLBCL after long-standing pyothorax ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/lymphomadiffusepyo.html))

## Clinical Issues

- **Epidemiology:**
  - Most common adult NHL (~30%); median age at diagnosis is seventh decade; occurs at all ages ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/lymphomadiffuse.html))
- **Sites:**
  - Involves nodal and extranodal sites: lymph node is most common
  - Bone marrow involvement in ~16%; increases risk of CNS relapse
  - Extranodal involvement (71% ≥1 site), 40% purely extranodal; GI tract is the most frequent extranodal site (18%)
  - Classic cases: can present as large mass in pleura (with chronic inflammation) or kidney ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/lymphomadiffuse.html))
- **Presentation:**
  - Rapidly enlarging mass (≥5 cm in 76% cases)
  - B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss) present in ~33%
  - Asymptomatic or incidentally found during workup of another process, including transformation of existing lymphomas (follicular, CLL/SLL, marginal zone, nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma)
  - Elevated LDH (53%)
- **Natural history:**
  - Aggressive; can be rapidly fatal if untreated
- **Treatment:**
  - R-CHOP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone) or other rituximab-based regimens ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/lymphomadiffuse.html))

## Staging

- Not specifically detailed in the evidence, but Ann Arbor staging and IPI (International Prognostic Index) are referenced under prognostic factors ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/lymphomadiffuse.html))

## Macroscopic

- Appearance depends on site but typically presents as a mass, often ≥5 cm
- Can present as masses in lymph node, pleura (especially associated with chronic inflammation/pyothorax), or kidney
- Pleural tumors may invade lung, diaphragm, mediastinum, or liver ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/lymphomadiffusepyo.html), [Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/lymphomadiffuse.html))

## Microscopic

- Diffuse architectural effacement by sheets of medium to large atypical lymphoid cells
- Cells have vesicular chromatin, prominent nucleoli; large cell defined as nucleus ≥ histiocyte or >2 lymphocyte nuclei
- Centroblastic variant: 2–4 nucleoli; Immunoblastic variant: single central nucleolus
![Typical DLBCL cytology in tonsil](https://storage.googleapis.com/pathology-hub-0/WHO/WHO_PICS/PEDS/18960.jpg)
![DLBCL: cytologic features](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/imgau/lymphomadiffuseklairmont02.jpg)
  - Anaplastic variant: bizarre, pleomorphic nuclei, may mimic ALCL or Reed-Sternberg cells
  - Plasmablastic and anaplastic morphologies possible; plasmablastic variant can resemble ALK+ large B cell lymphoma, requires ALK immunostain ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/lymphomadiffuse.html))
- Geographic necrosis, angioinvasion, and \"starry sky\" pattern may be present in some cases
![DLBCL, NOS: diffuse growth pattern](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/imgau/lymphomadiffuseklairmont01.jpg)

## Cytology

- Fine needle aspiration: large atypical lymphoid cells with vesicular chromatin and prominent nucleoli
- Cytology alone is insufficient; diagnosis of DLBCL-NOS requires immunophenotyping and cytogenetic studies ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/lymphomadiffuse.html))
- Flow cytometry is important adjunct: shows a monoclonal B cell population with high forward scatter (large size) ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/lymphomadiffuse.html))
![DLBCL: flow cytometry scatter plot](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/imgau/lymphomadiffuseklairmont07.jpg)

## Ancillary Tests

- **Immunohistochemistry:**
  - Pan B-cell markers: CD20, PAX5, CD79a, CD19, CD22 (positive)
  - Subtyping markers:
    - CD10 (30–50%, GCB), BCL6 (60–90%), MUM1 (35–65%) ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/lymphomadiffuse.html))
    - BCL2 (47–84%), MYC (>40% in double expressor)
    - CD30 (14%, often anaplastic morphology)
    - CD5 (12%)
    - Cyclin D1 negative in >98% (important to rule out mantle cell lymphoma; rare positive cases must lack t(11;14) and CD5 negativity)
    - TdT and ALK negative
    - CD3 negative
  - Hans algorithm: combines CD10, BCL6, MUM1 for COO subtyping
  - EBER ISH: >80% positive cells reclassifies as EBV+ DLBCL, NOS ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/lymphomadiffuse.html))
- **Molecular/genetics:**
  - FISH for MYC, BCL2, BCL6 rearrangements to rule out HGBL
  - Clonal immunoglobulin gene rearrangement by PCR
  - Gene expression profiling (GCB vs ABC), if available
  - Mutations: KMT2D, MYD88, PIM1, CREBBP, TP53, etc.
- **Flow cytometry:**
  - Identifies clonal, large, monoclonal B-cell population with high forward scatter

## Differential Diagnosis

| Entity                                             | Key Features                                                                                                       | IHC/Molecular Markers                                            |
|----------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------|
| High-grade B cell lymphoma, MYC/BCL2/BCL6 rearr.   | Aggressive, complex karyotype; must be excluded before DLBCL-NOS diagnosis; \"double/triple hit\" by FISH           | MYC and BCL2 and/or BCL6 rearrangements (FISH)                   |
| Burkitt lymphoma                                   | Medium cells, high mitoses, starry sky pattern, Ki-67 ~100%, CD10+, BCL6+, MYC+, BCL2 negative/weak; simple karyotype| MYC rearrangement only; BCL2/BCL6 not rearranged                 |
| Primary mediastinal (thymic) large B-cell lymphoma | Bulky anterior mediastinal mass, young adults, CD23+, PDL1+, MAL+, lack of surface Ig light chain, no systemic disease| CD23+, PDL1+, MAL+; surface Ig light chain negative              |
| EBV+ DLBCL, NOS                                    | >80% EBER+ cells; sheets of large cells, necrosis, angioinvasion, elderly; may be nodal/extranodal                  | EBER ISH+; EBV DNA in serum; often CD30+                         |
| T cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma       | Scattered large B-cells (<10%) in extensive T-cell/histiocyte background                                           | Minority CD20+ B-cells amid T-cell-rich background               |
| ALK+ large B-cell lymphoma                        | Plasmablastic morphology; ALK+, CD20-, CD30-; must be ruled out                                                    | ALK+; CD20-; CD30-; EBER-                                        |
| Mantle cell lymphoma (blastoid/pleomorphic)        | Cyclin D1+; may express CD5; t(11;14); blastoid cells can mimic DLBCL                                              | Cyclin D1+; SOX11+; t(11;14)                                     |
| Primary effusion lymphoma / HHV8+ DLBCL            | Body cavity involvement, immunodeficiency, HHV8+                                                                   | HHV8+; often negative for pan-B-cell markers                     |
| Follicular lymphoma, grade 3                       | Follicular architecture, CD21+/CD23+ FDC meshworks retained                                                        | Retained follicular dendritic cell network                       |
| Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma                | Large lymphoma cells confined to vessel lumina; may have CNS/skin symptoms                                         | CD20+; vessel-confined; diagnosis requires awareness              |
| Primary cutaneous DLBCL, leg type                  | Cutaneous mass, especially on leg; age often elderly; no systemic disease at diagnosis                             | CD20+, BCL2+, MUM1+/BCL6-, often high Ki-67                      |
| Lymphomatoid granulomatosis                        | Angiocentric/angiodestructive infiltrates; nearly always lungs; EBV+ B cells                                       | EBV+; T-cell/histiocytic background; B-cell markers on large cells|
| EBV positive mucocutaneous ulcer                   | Well circumscribed ulcer of oropharynx/skin in immunosuppressed; EBV+ large B cells                                | EBER ISH+; usually localized; indolent                           |

- ALK+ large B cell lymphoma: ALK+ status distinguishes from DLBCL, NOS, especially for plasmablastic morphology ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/lymphomadiffuse.html))
- PMBCL: Consider CD23, PDL1, MAL immunostains and clinical context (mediastinal presentation, young adult) to distinguish from DLBCL, NOS ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/lymphomadiffuse.html))
- EBER ISH positivity (>80%) reclassifies as EBV+ DLBCL, NOS ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/lymphomadiffuse.html))
- If MYC and BCL2 and/or BCL6 rearrangements by FISH, diagnose as HGBL ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/lymphomadiffuse.html))

## Prognostic Factors

- International Prognostic Index (IPI): incorporates age, LDH, ECOG ≥2, Ann Arbor stage III/IV, extranodal disease, bulky disease ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/lymphomadiffuse.html))
- Cell-of-origin: GCB subtype (5-year PFS 70–80%) vs ABC subtype (40–50%)
- MYC translocation: adverse prognosis
- Double expresser status (MYC ≥40% and BCL2 ≥50% by IHC, but no rearrangement): increased CNS relapse, worse survival
- Bone marrow involvement confers increased risk of CNS relapse

## Illustrative Cases

- 50-year-old man with chest pain
- 61-year-old man with B symptoms and leukocytosis
- 61-year-old woman with lung nodule
- 63-year-old man with dysphagia
- 67-year-old man with ptosis and blurry vision ([Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/lymphomadiffuse.html))

This section focuses on PMBCL and its differential diagnosis with these lymphomas, as the other diseases and systemic lymphomas involving the thymus, the commonest of which is diffuse large B-cell lymphoma NOS (DLBCL-NOS), are discussed elsewhere in this volume. PMBCL is a mature aggressive B-cell lymphoma of putative thymic B-cell origin, arising in the anterior mediastinum. It represents 2–3% of all non-Hodgkin lymphomas. Familial clustering of PMBCL cases has been reported based on shared genetic mutations. PMBCL occurs predominantly in young adults in their third decade, with a female predominance of 2:1, but it can also occur in children. Patients commonly present with cough, dyspnoea, and/or dysphagia, and many patients have bulky anterior mediastinal masses that can be associated with the superior vena cava syndrome. cards.title: Peripheral T-cell lymphoma NOS
cards.excerpt: Entity: Peripheral T-cell lymphoma NOS Section: microscopic PTCL-NOS can cause complete or partial effacement of the lymph node architecture. In most cases the pattern is diffuse, with medium to large pleomorphic cells. Less common cases with pleomorphic small and large cells are also described [[WHO Classification of Tumours Editorial Board. Haematolymphoid tumours. Lyon (France): International Agency for Research on Cancer; 2024. (WHO classification of tumours series, 5th ed.; vol. 11). https://publications.iarc.who.int/637.]]. Small lymphocytes, eosinophils, plasma cells, and histiocytes are present in the background. Haemophagocytosis can occasionally be detected. Residual atrophic follicles can be present. Clustered and scattered epithelioid histiocytes are frequently seen. Proliferations of high endothelial venules and follicular dendritic cells, which are seen characteristically in nodal TFH cell lymphoma, angioimmunoblastic type (nTFHL-AI) (previously known as angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma [AITL]), are not prominent in PTCL-NOS. cards.title: KSHV/HHV8-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
cards.excerpt: Entity: KSHV/HHV8-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma definition: Kaposi sarcoma–associated herpesvirus / human herpesvirus 8 (KSHV/HHV8)-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is a large B-cell lymphoma consistently associated with KSHV/HHV8, in general arising in patients with profound immunodeficiency, but it may occur in non-immunocompromised patients. The tumour cells morphologically resemble plasmablasts or immunoblasts and have abundant cytoplasmic IgM. related_terminology: Acceptable: HHV8-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma NOS. Not recommended: large B-cell lymphoma arising in HHV8-associated multicentric Castleman disease (obsolete). essential_and_desirable_diagnostic_criteria: Essential: presentation with primary nodal and/or splenic involvement; effacement of architecture by large blasts / transformed B cells with generally plasmablastic, immunoblastic, or anaplastic morphology; positive immunostaining for LANA (KSHV/HHV8) and IgM. Desirable: absence of immunoglobulin somatic hypermutations; EBER in situ hybridization (usually negative but can be positive in some cases).

cards.title: Peripheral T-cell lymphoma NOS
cards.excerpt: Entity: Peripheral T-cell lymphoma NOS definition: Peripheral T-cell lymphoma NOS (PTCL-NOS) is a heterogeneous category of mature T-cell lymphomas that do not correspond to any of the specifically defined entities of mature T-cell lymphomas. related_terminology: Not recommended: T-cell lymphoma NOS; peripheral T-cell lymphoma, pleomorphic small cell; peripheral T-cell lymphoma, pleomorphic medium and large cell; peripheral T-cell lymphoma, large cell; Lennert lymphoma. essential_and_desirable_diagnostic_criteria: Essential: a mass-forming clonal T-cell proliferation with a variable histological appearance; exclusion of immunodeficiency-associated lymphoproliferative disorders other than lymphoma; exclusion of specific T-cell lymphomas (i.e. lymphoblastic lymphoma, anaplastic large cell lymphoma, EBV-associated lymphoma/lymphoproliferation, and cutaneous T-cell lymphomas). Desirable: involvement of more than one site; aberrant T-cell phenotype confirming neoplastic nature.

cards.title: Peripheral T-cell lymphoma NOS
cards.excerpt: Entity: Peripheral T-cell lymphoma NOS definition: Peripheral T-cell lymphoma (PTCL) not otherwise specified (PTCL-NOS) is a heterogeneous category of nodal and extranodal mature T-cell lymphomas that cannot be assigned to a specific PTCL entity, consisting of a broad cytomorphological spectrum of medium to large lymphoid cells with variable degrees of pleomorphism.

cards.title: Splenic B-cell lymphoma
cards.excerpt: Entity: Splenic B-cell lymphoma definition: Primary splenic B-cell lymphomas (PSLs) are subtypes of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) and include the primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, which in the fifth edition of the WHO classification of haematolymphoid tumours has been renamed diffuse large B-cell lymphoma NOS (DLBCL-NOS), and four small B-cell lymphomas: hairy cell leukaemia (HCL), splenic marginal zone lymphoma (SMZL), splenic diffuse red pulp small B-cell lymphoma (SDRPL), and splenic B-cell lymphoma/leukaemia with prominent nucleoli (SBLPN).

cards.title: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma NOS
cards.excerpt: Entity: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma NOS definition: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma NOS (DLBCL-NOS) is a neoplasm of mature blastic B cells with a diffuse growth pattern. DLBCL-NOS encompasses all cases that do not belong to a specific diagnostic category of large B-cell lymphomas. related_terminology: None essential_and_desirable_diagnostic_criteria: Essential: architectural effacement by a diffuse proliferation of medium or large lymphoid cells with centroblastic or immunoblastic morphology; mature B-cell immunophenotype, TdT-negative; high Ki-67 index (but < 95%). Desirable: absence of MYC rearrangements; genetic testing, if relevant.

cards.title: DLBCL, NOS — Prognostic factors
cards.excerpt:
Unfavorable prognostic features:
Clinical: ↑ age, ↑ LDH, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) ≥ 2, Ann Arbor stage III / IV, extranodal disease, bulky disease (J Clin Oncol 2010;28:2373, Blood 2014;123:837)
Cell of origin status (Blood 2004;103:275):
Activated B cell subtype (~40%) and germinal center B cell subtype (~60%) associated with 5 year progression free survival rates of 40 - 50% versus 70 - 80%, respectively
MYC translocation (Blood 2015;126:2466)
Double expresser status: immunohistochemical coexpression of MYC (≥ 40% tumor cells) and BCL2 (≥ 50% tumor cells) in the absence of co-occurring MYC and BCL2 rearrangements

cards.title: DLBCL, NOS — DLBCL involving the kidney
cards.excerpt:
Frozen section description
Large atypical lymphoid cells with a diffuse growth pattern consistent with a large cell lymphoma can be appreciated on frozen sections; however, ancillary immunophenotypic and cytogenetic studies are required to establish B cell lineage and further differentiate specific DLBCL subtypes

cards.title: DLBCL, NOS — Microscopic (histologic) description
cards.excerpt:
Partial or complete effacement of normal tissue architecture by a diffuse infiltrate of large (or occasionally medium size) atypical B lymphoid cells with vesicular chromatin and prominent nucleoli
Large is defined as nucleus size ≥ histiocyte nucleus or > 2 lymphocyte nuclei

cards.title: DLBCL, NOS — Germinal center B cell (GCB) subtype: CD10+ or CD10- / BCL6+ / MUM1-
cards.excerpt:
Non-GCB subtype (classifier that encompasses ABC subtype and unclassifiable cases by GEP): CD10- / BCL6- or CD10- / BCL6+ / MUM1+
Double expresser status (30% of DLBCL, NOS):
Positive staining for BCL2 (> 50% tumor cells) and MYC (> 40% tumor cells) in the absence of underlying chromosomal rearrangements (double expresser) is associated with increased risk of CNS relapse and inferior survival (J Clin Oncol 2017;35:2515)
If MYC and BCL2 rearrangements confirmed by FISH, classified as high grade B cell lymphoma with MYC and BCL2 rearrangements (also known as double hit DLBCL)

cards.title: DLBCL, NOS — Scatter plots of splenic massMolecular / cytogenetics description
cards.excerpt:
Gene expression profiling identifies activated B cell and germinal center B cell molecular subtypes of DLBCL, NOS
Since gene expression profiling is not widely available in the clinical setting, immunohistochemical algorithms that approximate these molecular subtypes (i.e., Hans algorithm) are used as an alternative (see Immunohistochemical subclassification)
FISH used to differentiate DLBCL, NOS from high grade B cell lymphoma with MYC and BCL2 and / or BCL6 rearrangements:
BCL2 rearrangement (20 - 30%; < 5% activated B cell, 50% germinal center B cell)
BCL6 rearrangement (30%; 30% activated B cell, 15% germinal center B cell)
MYC rearrangement (8 - 14% for activated B cell and germinal center B cell; ~50% have co-occurring BCL2 or BCL6 rearrangement)

Gene expression profiling identifies activated B cell and germinal center B cell molecular subtypes of DLBCL, NOS
Since gene expression profiling is not widely available in the clinical setting, immunohistochemical algorithms that approximate these molecular subtypes (i.e., Hans algorithm) are used as an alternative (see Immunohistochemical subclassification)
FISH used to differentiate DLBCL, NOS from high grade B cell lymphoma with MYC and BCL2 and / or BCL6 rearrangements:
BCL2 rearrangement (20 - 30%; < 5% activated B cell, 50% germinal center B cell)
BCL6 rearrangement (30%; 30% activated B cell, 15% germinal center B cell)
MYC rearrangement (8 - 14% for activated B cell and germinal center B cell; ~50% have co-occurring BCL2 or BCL6 rearrangement)

cards.title: DLBCL, NOS — PCR B cell gene rearrangement studies show clonal immunoglobulin gene rearrangement
cards.excerpt:
Mutational landscape very heterogeneous with recurrent alterations identified in over 150 genes
Most frequently mutated genes include KMT2D (25%), MYD88 (17%), PIM1 (15%), CREBBP (12%), HIST1H1E (11%), BCL2 (10%), SPEN (10%), ARID1A (10%), TP53 (9%) (Cell 2017;171:481)
Multiple integrative genomic classification models recently proposed but none currently incorporated into WHO classification guidelines (Cell 2017;171:481, N Engl J Med 2018;378:1396, Nat Med 2018;24:679, Blood 2020;135:1759)
Common DLBCL genomic subtypes that have emerged from multiple independent studies include those characterized by:
MYD88 L265P and CD79B mutations: mainly activated B cell subtype, 18q gain, genetically similar to primary extranodal lymphomas, poor survival
BCL6 translocations and NOTCH2 mutations: mainly activated B cell subtype, constitutive B cell receptor signaling, genetically similar to marginal zone lymphoma, more favorable survival
BCL2 translocations and mutations in EZH2 / other chromatin modifiers: mostly germinal center B cell subtype with genetic features similar to other B cell lymphomas of germinal center origin

cards.title: DLBCL, NOS — Lymph node, left cervical, excisional biopsy
cards.excerpt:
Diffuse large B cell lymphoma, NOS, GCB subtype (see comment)
Comment: H&E sections show effacement of the normal nodal architecture by sheets of large atypical lymphoid cells with vesicular chromatin and prominent nucleoli. By immunohistochemistry, the tumor cells are positive for CD20, CD10 and BCL6, while negative for CD3, CD5, MUM1, BCL2, MYC and cyclin D1. EBER ISH is negative. The Ki67 proliferation index is 70%. Cytogenetic FISH studies are negative for rearrangements of BCL2, BCL6 and MYC. The morphologic, immunophenotypic and cytogenetic findings are diagnostic of diffuse large B cell lymphoma, NOS, GCB subtype (Hans algorithm).

cards.title: EBV+ DLBCL — Prognostic data derived mainly from retrospective studies
cards.excerpt:
Worse prognosis in older patients (> 45 years)
In elderly patients > 70 years, B symptoms are associated with worse prognosis
Monomorphic EBV positive diffuse large B cell lymphoma associated with worse prognosis in younger patients as compared with cases with T histiocyte rich or polymorphic large B cell patterns
Prognosis varies with region (Asian data is controversial) (Blood 2013;122:328)

cards.title: EBV+ DLBCL — Treatment
cards.excerpt:
No prospective comparative studies have been performed to evaluate treatment options
No standard approach, treatment strategies similar to de novo EBV negative diffuse large B cell lymphoma
R-CHOP, with overall response rates of 50 - 90% and complete response rates of 30 - 70% (Am J Hematol 2018;93:953)

Canonical large B cell-like features: high density of large neoplastic cells and scattered Reed-Sternberg-like cells

cards.title: EBV+ DLBCL — Lymph node, cervical lymph node, excision
cards.excerpt:
EBV positive, diffuse large B cell lymphoma
Microscopic description: The lymph node architecture is completely effaced by a variably sized infiltrate, including very large cells with irregular nuclear membranes, vesicular nuclei, distinct nucleoli and moderate amount of cytoplasm. There is a mixed infiltrate composed of small lymphocytes and histiocytes. The background is hyalinized, with areas of necrosis and foreign body giant cells. There are areas with residual small lymphocytes.
Immunostains: The large neoplastic cells are positive for CD20, PAX5, CD30 and negative for CD15 and CD10. BCL6 stains a subset of the large cells. EBER and LMP1 are positive in the large cells. CD3 and CD5 stain the background small T cells. Ki67 stains the majority of the large cells with an overall staining of approximately 50%.

cards.title: DLBCL / high grade B cell lymphoma with MYC and BCL2 rearrangements — Prognostic factors
cards.excerpt:
Relatively low response rate with R-CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisone, plus the monoclonal antibody rituximab) with short overall survival (4.5 - 18.5 months), prompting investigation of alternative therapeutic approaches (J Clin Oncol 2010;28:3360, Blood 2015;126:2466)
MYC partner: MYC / IG translocation may have a worse outcome compared to non-IG partner in some studies although this remains an area of investigation (Blood 2015;126:2466, Haematologica 2014;99:726)
Tumor morphology (may warrant further study, per WHO): majority of double hit lymphomas have DLBCL morphology and can be indistinguishable morphologically

cards.title: DLBCL / high grade B cell lymphoma with MYC and BCL2 rearrangements — DLBCL, NOS: large nuclei, low proliferation rate, low rate of MYC rearrangement
cards.excerpt:
DLBCL, NOS with double expresser phenotype: while double hit lymphomas are also generally double expressers, the majority of these are activated B cell subtype DLBCL and do not harbor translocations (Hematology Am Soc Hematol Educ Program 2014;2014:9)
Burkitt Lymphoma: medium size nuclei, high proliferation rate (Ki67 100%), weak or absent BCL2 expression, negative for BCL2 translocation; cytoplasmic vacuoles can be seen on touch imprints (often absent in double hit)
Burkitt-like lymphoma with 11q aberration: similar histology to Burkitt, lacks MYC translocation, 11q aberration, weak or negative BCL2 expression, negative for BCL2 translocation
B lymphoblastic leukemia / lymphoma with MYC and BCL2 rearrangement: small blasts, TdT+, CD10+, BCL6-, CCND1-; may arise from follicular lymphoma (Hum Pathol 2015;46:260)
Mantle cell lymphoma, blastoid variant: medium size nuclei, cyclin D1+, presence of t(11;14) translocation
Richter syndrome: Similar histology to DLBCL, NOS with CD5+ B-cells, pretransformed CLL / SLL might be present
Follicular lymphoma, grade 3B with retained follicular architecture and presence of MYC translocation in addition to the underlying IGH-BCL2 translocation (Swerdlow: WHO Classification of Tumours of Haematopoietic and Lymphoid Tissues, 2017, Blood 2016;127:2375)

cards.title: KSHV / HHV8 positive diffuse large B cell lymphoma — Essential features
cards.excerpt:
Usually arises in association with multicentric Castleman disease (MCD) and HIV infection
Morphologically similar to plasmablasts but correspond to naïve IgM producing B cell without somatic hypermutations
Sheets of HHV8 latency associated nuclear antigen (LANA1) positive plasmablasts efface lymph node architecture
Atypical cells are strongly positive for cytoplasmic IgM with lambda light chain restriction and negative for EBV encoded small RNA (EBER)

cards.title: KSHV / HHV8 positive diffuse large B cell lymphoma — Epidemiology
cards.excerpt:
Rare disease with overall frequency of 0.1% (Leuk Lymphoma 2018;59:1375)
Median age is 47 years (range 39 - 66); M:F = 3.3:1 (Pathology 2020;52:53)
Usually arises in association with HHV8 positive multicentric Castleman disease (MCD) and HIV (15 times higher risk) (Blood 2002;99:2331)

cards.title: KSHV / HHV8 positive diffuse large B cell lymphoma — Pathophysiology
cards.excerpt:
HHV8 infects singly scattered cells that are morphologically similar to plasmablasts with abundant cytoplasmic immunoglobulin but are, in fact, naïve IgM producing B cells that lack IG somatic hypermutations and are polyclonal at the molecular level
HHV8 positive plasmablasts form aggregates (microlymphomas), which can be polyclonal or monoclonal (Am J Clin Pathol 2017;147:171)
HHV8 positive aggregates rarely can expand to HHV8 positive large B cell lymphoma, which is monoclonal

cards.title: KSHV / HHV8 positive diffuse large B cell lymphoma — Clinical features
cards.excerpt:
Usually manifests with profound immunodeficiency, enlarging lymph nodes and massive splenomegaly
There may be manifestations of Kaposi sarcoma (Blood 2002;99:2331)
Rarely, may arise in absence of MCD (Mod Pathol 2017;30:745)

cards.title: KSHV / HHV8 positive diffuse large B cell lymphoma — Microscopic (histologic) description
cards.excerpt:

missing_essentials: The Essential and Desirable Diagnostic Criteria section is missing: absence of TdT by immunohistochemistry (specifically stated in WHO and Pathology Outlines).
Macroscopic: The draft does not mention that DLBCL, NOS can present as a mass in the kidney or pleura as reflected in the illustrative and macroscopic images/cases.

Differential Diagnosis: The draft omits intravascular large B cell lymphoma and primary cutaneous DLBCL, leg type—both are explicitly listed as entities in the differential diagnosis section of Pathology Outlines.
Differential Diagnosis: Lymphomatoid granulomatosis is omitted, which is specified as a DLBCL mimic in evidence.
Differential Diagnosis: Plasmablastic morphology as a consideration for ALK+ large B cell lymphoma is not explicitly noted.

Cytology: The evidence includes flow cytometry findings and detail that the diagnosis should not be based on cytology alone, but requires immunophenotype and cytogenetic studies—this is stated, but the flow cytometry role should be cross-linked more clearly from the ancillary test section (not only in Ancillary, but in Cytology) per evidence structure.
Ancillary Tests: The draft does not mention that cyclin D1 is negative in the majority of DLBCL but included as a deployable marker to rule out mantle cell lymphoma as per Pathology Outlines.
Ancillary Tests: The draft does not include that EBER ISH positivity >80% reclassifies as EBV+ DLBCL, NOS.
Prognostic Factors: International Prognostic Index (IPI) is not mentioned, though the evidence refers to it specifically as influencing prognosis.
Clinical Issues: The draft should note that some cases are associated with transformation from nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma, as specified in the evidence.
Clinical Issues: The draft should also mention that an association exists with bone marrow involvement increasing CNS relapse risk.
Essential and Desirable Diagnostic Criteria: 'High proliferation index (Ki-67), typically high but <95%' is stated, but the WHO states "<95%" as a desirable, not absolute cutoff.
Differential Diagnosis: EBV positive mucocutaneous ulcer is omitted as a DLBCL mimic.
redundant: Key Facts bullet 'Prognosis and treatment responses vary by molecular subtype and double expresser/double hit status' repeats information also present at length in the Prognostic Factors section.

Essential and Desirable Diagnostic Criteria: 'Requires exclusion of high-grade B cell lymphoma (HGBL) with MYC and BCL2 and/or BCL6 rearrangements ("double/triple hit")' closely duplicates text later repeated in the same section.
confusing: In Differential Diagnosis table, it is not clear in what clinical context to use CD23, PDL1, and MAL for PMBCL versus other DLBCL; a clear marker/clinical role would help for PMBCL based on evidence.
figure_issues: The illustrative figure of flow cytometry scatter plot is placed only in the Ancillary Tests section, but the evidence and cytology description imply that flow cytometry should also illustrate or be referenced in the Cytology section.
critic_json.notes_for_revision: Add missing differential diagnosis entities (including intravascular large B cell lymphoma, primary cutaneous DLBCL leg type, EBV positive mucocutaneous ulcer, and lymphomatoid granulomatosis). Move the role of flow cytometry to both Cytology and Ancillary Tests. Add diagnostic criteria of cyclin D1 negativity, more clearly state the need for EBER ISH in diagnosis, and include macroscopic findings such as pleura/kidney. Remove redundant bullets between sections. Ensure IPI is referenced under Prognostic Factors and update clinical/transformation associations. Clarify marker roles in the DDx table for PMBCL.
